strengths: The paper is clearly written and the method is simple and well-motivated: conditioning a Marigold-style diffusion depth estimator on text captions to exploit the language prior in text-to-image pre-training is an intuitive idea, and the pipeline (Fig. 3) is easy to follow.

Experiments are fairly comprehensive: zero-shot evaluation on four standard benchmarks (NYUv2, KITTI, ETH3D, ScanNet) following the established affine-invariant protocol, plus convergence curves (Fig. 7), denoising-step analysis (Fig. 8 / Table 4), a small-region analysis using panoptic masks (Table 2), prompt ablations (Table 3), and a fallback analysis with blank/template text (Table 5).

The fallback analysis (Table 5) is honest and informative: it shows the improvement attributable to real text content over Marigold-like baselines and demonstrates the model still works with template prompts, partially addressing the practical concern that captions may be unavailable.
The small-area evaluation (Table 2) is a sensible way to test the claim that language guides attention to hard-to-see regions, and the results support a (modest) improvement where predicted.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported: training data, resolution, scheduler, batch size, GPU, caption generation procedure (LLaVA versions and prompts) are all specified, and code release is promised.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is thin. The method is essentially Marigold with text conditioning re-enabled—the CLIP text encoder path already exists in Stable Diffusion, and the 'contribution' amounts to feeding captions during fine-tuning and inference. No new architectural or training machinery is introduced.

The central hypothesis is not rigorously tested due to a circularity in the experimental design: all text at train and test time is generated by LLaVA from the very image being described. The paper argues language provides an independent prior resolving visual ambiguity (occlusion, texture ambiguity), but a VLM caption cannot contain information absent from the image; it is derived from the same ambiguous signal. The claimed 'human-provided prior' is never evaluated with actual human-written descriptions, nor against image-derived captions of degraded quality, so it is impossible to tell whether gains come from genuine geometric priors in language, from attention redistribution, or from simply another view of the same image features.

The measured gains over the directly comparable baseline (Marigold, same 74K training images) are marginal: e.g., NYUv2 95.9→96.0 δ1 / 6.0→5.9 AbsRel; KITTI 90.4→90.6 / 10.5→10.4; ScanNet 94.5→94.9 / 6.9→6.7. The re-implemented Marigold baseline also scores lower than the published Marigold numbers (95.7 vs 95.9 on NYUv2), and no error bars or significance tests are provided, so the differences may be within noise.

The abstract's claim of 'state-of-the-art zero-shot performance' is overstated. Depth Anything v2 substantially outperforms PriorDiffusion on NYUv2, KITTI, ETH3D, and ScanNet (e.g., 97.9/4.4 vs 96.0/5.9 on NYUv2) despite being listed in the same table; the paper is only competitive within the small-data regime.

Inconsistencies raise correctness concerns: in Table 4, the step-1 results are identical to four significant figures for Marigold and PriorDiffusion across all four datasets, which is implausible if text conditioning is active from the first denoising step and suggests a reporting or pipeline error. The depth normalization formula also differs in sign between Eq. (1) in the main text (y98 − y2) and Eq. (2) in the supplement (y2 − y98).

The 'faster inference trajectory' claim is modest in practical terms: convergence in 10 vs 25 DDIM steps is a useful but limited efficiency gain, and the training speedup (converging at 20K vs 30K iterations) comes with the extra cost of generating 740,000 LLaVA captions (740 GPU hours), which is not accounted for in the efficiency argument.

The 'user-intent / controllability' claims (contribution 2) rest on cherry-picked qualitative examples (Figs. 2, 4, 5, 6, 10, 11) without a user study or any quantitative controllability metric; the failure case (Fig. 9) showing that wrong text misleads the model further underlines the fragility of this behavior.

Presentation issues: repeated typos ('Margold', 'ground truch', 'Is shows'), duplicate template prompts B/C in Table 3, and an unfinished sentence 'Code will be released' with no punctuation in the abstract.

strengths: The core idea—injecting language descriptions into a Marigold-style diffusion depth estimator—is intuitive and clearly motivated, and the paper is easy to follow with a well-structured pipeline description.

The experimental protocol is reasonably comprehensive: training on two synthetic datasets with zero-shot evaluation on four real-world benchmarks (NYUv2, KITTI, ETH3D, ScanNet), following the established Marigold configuration and affine-invariant evaluation protocol.

The paper includes a genuine attempt at ablation and analysis: prompt ablations (Table 3), template-prompt comparison (Table 5), denoising-step sweeps (Table 4/Fig. 8), small-area evaluation (Table 2), and controllability/failure-case examples (Figs. 6, 9), plus honest discussion of limitations.
The faster-convergence claim is supported by concrete evidence (Fig. 7, Table 1), and the observation that fewer denoising steps suffice (10 vs. 25) is a useful practical finding.
Thorough supplementary material including dataset details, evaluation metric definitions, and caption-generation recipes, which supports reproducibility of the training pipeline.
weaknesses: The headline quantitative gains over Marigold are marginal and likely within run-to-run noise. E.g., NYUv2: 96.0/5.9 vs. 95.9/6.0; ScanNet: 94.9/6.7 vs. 94.5/6.9; and on KITTI (90.3/10.4) the method does not exceed the originally reported Marigold (90.4/10.5). No error bars, multiple seeds, or significance tests are provided, yet the abstract claims 'state-of-the-art zero-shot performance.'

The central hypothesis—that the 'language prior learned during text-to-image pretraining' provides an inductive bias about geometry—is not actually validated, and the paper's own ablations undermine it. Table 5 shows that with template prompts or blank text ('An image') the method degrades to Marigold-level performance (95.7/6.1 on NYUv2), meaning all gains disappear unless a full image caption is supplied. This suggests the improvement comes from conditioning on LLaVA's per-image semantic understanding rather than from any text-to-image-learned language prior; a caption from a VLM that sees the image is a fundamentally different signal from a generic language prior.

The evaluation is confounded by unequal test-time information and compute: PriorDiffusion at test time consumes LLaVA captions (3.6 s/image, plus 740 GPU-hours of captioning for training data), whereas Marigold uses only the image. The claims of better 'perception' are therefore not comparable at equal information, and the practical deployment scenario (a human providing descriptions per frame) is contrived and largely hypothetical.

Novelty is limited. Conditioning Stable Diffusion on text via a frozen CLIP encoder is a standard mechanism, and the related-work section itself lists closely related efforts (VPD, WorDepth, RSA, DepthCLIP) that already use language for depth. The contribution reduces to re-tokenizing Marigold with LLaVA captions.

The claimed 'state-of-the-art' positioning is inaccurate: Depth Anything v2 outperforms on NYUv2 (4.4 AbsRel) and ScanNet (4.2), and the paper's own Table 1 shows PriorDiffusion is essentially on par, not clearly superior, to Marigold under matched conditions.

The faster-training-convergence claim compares against the authors' own re-implemented Marigold checkpoints, whose numbers are below the published Marigold results, making the convergence advantage harder to assess against the reference method.
Small-area improvements (Table 2) are small (~1 point δ1) and again rely on VLM captions at test time, so the practical significance is unclear.

Writing has noticeable sloppiness (e.g., 'Margold,' 'visual nuisance' vs. 'nuisances,' 'ground truch,' broken equations/references in Sec. 3, an unfinished fragment in Fig. 9 discussion), which suggests the manuscript was not carefully polished.

strengths: The paper is technically sound in its execution: the pipeline is a clean extension of Marigold-style latent diffusion depth estimation, with the DDPM formulation, training objective, and inference procedure clearly specified, and implementation details (scheduler, iterations, batch size, hardware) reported at a level that supports reproducibility.

The evaluation is broad and follows established zero-shot protocols across four diverse benchmarks (NYUv2, KITTI, ETH3D, ScanNet), with affine-invariant metrics consistent with prior work, and a fair no-ensemble comparison against a re-implemented Marigold baseline.

The supplementary material contains genuinely useful ablations: denoising-step analysis (Table 4, converging in ~10 vs ~25 steps), template-prompt robustness (Tables 3 and 5), small-area analysis using panoptic masks (Table 2), and an honest failure-case discussion (Figure 9).
The claimed efficiency benefits—faster training convergence (Figure 7) and fewer inference steps—are practically valuable and are supported by both curves and tables.
The writing is generally clear, and the limitations section candidly acknowledges dependence on caption quality and the feasibility of user-provided text.
weaknesses: The quantitative evidence for the central claim is thin. Compared to the re-implemented Marigold baseline, the final gains are marginal and inconsistent: NYUv2 96.0 vs 95.9 δ1, KITTI 90.3 vs 90.4 δ1 (actually slightly worse at 30k iterations), ETH3D 95.8 vs 95.4. AbsRel differences are ~0.1-0.4. The 'state-of-the-art zero-shot performance' claim in the abstract is therefore overstated; the method is roughly on par with Marigold, not clearly better.

The core hypothesis—that language provides a geometric/semantic inductive bias—is not well isolated. In Table 5, a generic template like 'A complex 3D scene...' or even blank text achieves 95.5-95.8 on NYUv2 versus 96.0 with real captions, and 'An image' reaches 95.7. This suggests most of the improvement over Marigold comes from adding any text conditioning (possibly acting as regularization or extra context), not from scene-specific language priors. A direct ablation training with template captions instead of LLaVA captions is missing to separate these effects.

The 'better perception of described regions' and 'controllable depth estimation' claims rest on cherry-picked qualitative examples (Figures 2, 4, 5, 6, 10, 11). Table 2 evaluates small areas in general but does not correlate masks with objects actually mentioned in the text, so it does not verify the text-guided-attention mechanism.

Novelty is incremental: the architectural change (feeding a caption through the frozen CLIP text encoder of Stable Diffusion alongside the Marigold-style setup) is straightforward, and language-for-depth has been explored in DepthCLIP, WorDepth, RSA, and VPD. The contribution is a new application rather than a new technique or significant insight.

Test-time dependence on a VLM (LLaVA captions generated from the test images) adds inference cost and complexity that is not accounted for in the efficiency claims; the practical deployment story (a user must describe each image, or a captioner must run first) is acknowledged but unresolved.

Presentation issues that should be corrected: repeated typos ('Margold', 'ground truch', 'Is shows', 'nuisance' for 'nuisance'-type errors), duplicate template definitions in Table 3 (Templates B and C are identical), and inconsistent caption/baseline naming. These do not affect the science but indicate a lack of polish.

There is no comparison to, or discussion of compute cost versus, other fast diffusion depth methods (e.g., DepthFM, Lotus, GenPercept) that specifically target few-step inference, so the practical significance of the 10-step convergence is hard to judge.

strengths: The paper systematically investigates an under-explored question: whether language can serve as an additional conditioning signal for diffusion-based monocular depth estimation. The experimental breadth is commendable — three diffusion depth estimators (Marigold, Lotus, E2E-FT) with multiple variants, two synthetic training datasets, and five zero-shot evaluation benchmarks.

The ablations are unusually thorough: text at train-only vs. infer-only vs. both, prompt templates for caption generation (Tables 3, 5), number of captions per image (Table 6), denoising steps (Table 4), and small-area evaluation via panoptic masks (Table 2). These go beyond a single headline number and characterize when and where text helps.

The findings are practically interesting: faster training convergence (Figure 7), fewer denoising steps needed at inference (converges at ~10 steps vs. 25 for the baseline, Table 4), and consistent gains on small regions (Table 2, δ1 92.8 vs 91.7 at 5% area). These could be valuable for efficiency as well as accuracy.

The paper is transparent about failure modes: it shows that incorrect text misguides the model (Figure 9), reports non-reproducible baseline results in gray, and honestly notes cases where text integration hurts (e.g., Lotus-G). This transparency increases trust.

The hypothesis is well-motivated: text-to-image pre-training implicitly encodes object size, shape, and spatial relationships, and the paper articulates how this reduces the depth solution space for ambiguous regions.
weaknesses: The quantitative improvements are modest, mixed, and not shown to be statistically significant. Several Train&Infer configurations are worse than their text-free baselines (e.g., Lotus-G+Text NYUv2 δ1 96.3 vs. Lotus-G 96.8; ETH3D 96.3 vs. 97.0), and the re-trained baselines differ from published numbers (e.g., Marigold* 95.7 vs. 95.9), suggesting the gains may be within training variance. No repeated runs or error bars are reported, so it is difficult to judge how robust the improvements are.

The experimental setup is inconsistent across the three backbone methods: LLaVA v1.6 with 10 captions per image for Marigold, but InternVL3-8B with a single caption for Lotus and E2E-FT. This confounds cross-method conclusions — differences in how much text helps may be attributable to the captioning model/quantity rather than the underlying depth estimator.

The method is technically straightforward: concatenating frozen CLIP text embeddings with depth latents, following standard DDPM training. The novelty lies in the empirical finding rather than any new technique or formulation, which limits the technical contribution relative to CVPR's bar.

The mechanism claim (language reduces the solution space because text-to-image pre-training encodes 3D scene structure) is plausible but not directly validated. No attention analysis, probing, or counterfactual experiment demonstrates that the model actually uses the text's geometric content; the evidence is largely correlational (overall metric improvements and cherry-picked visualizations).

Practical applicability is under-quantified: at inference time, every image requires a VLM caption, whose generation cost (740 GPU hours for Marigold training captions alone) and latency are non-trivial, yet no end-to-end runtime comparison is provided. The claim that language comes 'at no additional cost' in embodied-agent settings is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The improvements rely on VLM-generated captions that may hallucinate or omit scene details (the paper itself shows wrong text misguides the model); there is no analysis of caption error rates on the synthetic training data or of how robustness degrades as caption quality drops beyond a single qualitative example.

Some writing issues: the formulation section largely restates standard DDPM machinery; the related-work section contains a duplicated reference ([84]/[85] same title); and the '1, 3, 4' style page back-references appear misplaced. These are presentation-level issues but reflect insufficient polish.

strengths: The paper conducts a broad empirical study: the language-conditioning strategy is applied consistently across three diffusion-based depth estimators (Marigold, Lotus, E2E-FT) and evaluated zero-shot on five standard benchmarks, giving the empirical claims reasonable breadth.

Several useful ablations are provided: prompt templates for caption generation (Table 3), denoising-step convergence (Table 4), fixed template prompts at inference (Table 5), number of captions per image (Table 6), and small-region analysis via panoptic masks (Table 2).

The authors are transparent about reproducibility: they gray out results not reproducible with released code and clearly mark retrained baselines, and they honestly document the failure mode when incorrect text is supplied (Figure 9).

The core hypothesis — that text-to-image pre-training endows the diffusion model with a usable language-conditional prior that can regularize depth estimation — is plausible and the training/inference-only ablations (which still show slight gains) are an interesting observation.
Implementation details, dataset protocols, and metrics are described thoroughly in the supplementary material, supporting reproducibility once code is released.
weaknesses: The quantitative gains are marginal and inconsistent. In Table 1, 'Marigold + Text (Train & Infer)' improves AbsRel on NYUv2 only 6.0→5.9 and δ1 not at all; several with-text variants actually degrade relative to the original published baselines (e.g., Lotus-G + Text 96.3/5.9 vs. original Lotus-G 96.8/5.4 on NYUv2; E2E-FT + Text 96.3/6.2 vs. 96.5/5.4). No statistical significance tests, variance over seeds, or multiple-comparison analysis are provided to support claims that small deltas are real.

A fundamental circularity is not addressed: the text conditions are generated by vision-language models (LLaVA, InternVL3-8B) that themselves only see the input image. The captions therefore encode little if any information beyond the visual signal, weakening the central narrative that language 'reduces the solution space' by injecting extra-visual 3D knowledge. The observed gains may largely reflect an auxiliary regularizer or text-embedding regularization effect rather than genuine language-grounded disambiguation.

The method itself is technically simple — feeding CLIP text embeddings as an additional condition into existing pipelines — with limited novelty relative to prior language-for-depth work the paper cites (WorDepth, RSA, DepthCLIP, VPD).

The reported cost is very high relative to the benefit: 740 GPU hours just to caption the training set for Marigold, plus retraining, for improvements that are often within noise and sometimes negative.

Key supporting analyses are thin: the 'faster convergence' claim rests on single-run curves on a subset of data (Figure 7); the iterative refinement result (Figure 6) is a hand-curated example where sentences are appended and inference simply re-run, with no quantitative protocol; and the small-area analysis in Table 2 uses baseline numbers (95.7/6.1) inconsistent with the main table (95.9/5.9), making cross-table comparisons confusing.

Several results in Table 1 (e.g., 'Train Only' and 'Infer Only' rows that sometimes hurt) complicate the paper's own findings, yet the findings summary (Findings 1–3) presents them mostly as positive observations without careful analysis of when and why language helps or hurts.

Only Marigold is analyzed in depth (denoising steps, convergence); the conclusions about language as a 'constraint accelerating the diffusion trajectory' are not shown to hold for Lotus or E2E-FT, limiting generality of the stated findings.

strengths: The paper conducts a systematic, broad empirical study of a timely question: whether language conditioning improves diffusion-based monocular depth estimation. Testing across three representative architectures (Marigold, Lotus, E2E-FT) with multiple variants, two synthetic training sets, and five zero-shot evaluation benchmarks lends credibility to the conclusions.

The decomposition into Train-Only, Infer-Only, and Train-&-Infer settings is a thoughtful ablation. The observation that gains persist even when text is available at only one of the two stages (with a plausible explanation grounded in text-to-image pre-training priors) is one of the more interesting findings.

Beyond aggregate metrics, the paper provides several targeted analyses: faster training convergence (Fig. 7), fewer denoising steps needed at inference (Fig. 8, Table 4 — convergence at 10 vs 25 steps), improved perception of small regions using MaskDINO-derived masks (Table 2), iterative refinement with progressively detailed captions (Fig. 6), and a failure analysis with wrong text (Fig. 9). This breadth of evidence supports the qualitative claims.

The supplementary material is thorough: prompt ablations (Tables 3, 5), caption-count ablation (Table 6), detailed training configurations, and evaluation protocol, which supports reproducibility. The authors also transparently gray out non-reproducible published baselines rather than silently mixing numbers.
The paper is honest about limitations (dependence on caption quality, risk of misleading text) and about its framing as an empirical investigation rather than a new architecture.
weaknesses: The quantitative gains are small and, in several cases, marginal: e.g., Marigold NYUv2 δ1 95.7→95.9 and AbsRel 6.1→5.9; KITTI δ1 89.7→90.6. No statistical significance testing, seed variance, or per-image paired analysis is provided, so it is difficult to judge whether these differences are robust rather than noise, particularly given the sensitivity of diffusion fine-tuning.

Some results are inconsistent or raise reproducibility concerns: the retrained Lotus-G baseline (95.2/6.7) differs substantially from the published number (96.8/5.4), and several Train-Only / Infer-Only variants actually degrade performance relative to the baseline (e.g., Lotus-D Train-Only on ScanNet: 95.1 vs 96.0; Marigold Train-Only on ScanNet: 92.6 vs 94.0). In Table 4, the 1-step rows are identical to the decimal for baseline and text models, which is surprising if text conditioning is active at inference and is not explained.

Novelty is limited: the core method is essentially re-enabling/finetuning with the CLIP text branch that Stable Diffusion already possesses. The mechanistic hypothesis (text-to-image pre-training encodes 3D-conditional structure) is stated but not directly verified, e.g., no probing, attention analysis, or controlled experiments isolating what text actually contributes versus simple caption-induced regularization (which could act as an additional augmentation/regularizer).

Captions are generated by VLMs (LLaVA, InternVL3) rather than humans, so the claim that language supplies 'conditions aligned with plausible 3D scenes at no additional cost' is weakened: at test time a VLM captioning pass is required (or a template fallback, which recovers only part of the gain), and the gains may partly reflect properties of VLM-generated text rather than genuine 3D knowledge transfer. Evaluation with real human descriptions would strengthen the claim.

There is no quantitative comparison against prior language-for-depth methods (e.g., WorDepth, RSA) or against language-conditioned dense prediction approaches, making it hard to position the contribution relative to existing uses of text for depth.

Evaluation is affine-invariant (scale/shift aligned), which masks exactly the kind of scene-level metric reasoning language is claimed to provide (absolute sizes, spatial layout); a metric-depth or scale-aware evaluation would test the central hypothesis more directly. Relatedly, the 'Train Only' gains reported in the introduction as a notable finding are small and inconsistent across datasets/architectures, and the paper offers only speculative explanations.

Presentation has a number of errors that should be corrected: typos ('ground truch', 'Is shows', 'we Marigold baseline and'), duplicated/near-duplicate references ([83] vs [85] are the same work listed as arXiv and conference versions; [41]/[42] share an arXiv number), and a name mismatch between the paper title 'Iris' and the supplementary figure captions referring to 'PriorDiffusion'.
